chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl bin Ziyad and Ahmad bin Muhammad, Ziyad and Ahmad bin Muhammad, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abu Ayoub, from Sama'ah who said:

I said to Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him): 'A man from us has something with him to meet his expenses with, and upon him is a debt. Should he feed his family until Allah, Mighty and Majestic, grants him ease so he could fulfill his debt, or should he borrow upon his back in bad times and difficult earning, or accept charity?'
He (peace be upon him) said: 'He should fulfill his debt with whatever is with him, and he should not consume the wealth of the people except that with him is what he can pay their rights to them.'
Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is saying: 'And do not swallow up your property among yourselves by false means, except if there happens to be a compromising trade among you.'
And he should not borrow upon his back except that there is fulfillment with him.

And if he was to go around the doors of the people, they would return him with the morsel and the two morsels, and a date and two dates, unless if there happens to be a guardian for him who would fulfill his debts from after him. There is none from us who dies except Allah, Mighty and Majestic, Makes a guardian for him who would stand with regards to his promises and his debts, so he would fulfill his promises and his debts.
ai.seo_question: What should a Muslim do with their assets if they have outstanding debts?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the hierarchy of financial obligations, prioritizing debt repayment over consumption to prevent unjustly consuming others' wealth, a principle rooted in the Quranic prohibition of 'akl al-mal bi'l-batil'. It further establishes the practical legal mechanism where a designated wali ensures the deceased's debts and waiting period (iddah) are settled, reflecting the Shia emphasis on financial integrity and social responsibility.
